findings.detail: Root cause: the two layers were being compared inside different stacking contexts, so the larger z-index lost. The review column carries isolate, which creates a stacking context of its own, and the toast wrapper lived inside that column at z-40. The sticky filter bar sits one level up at z-20, a sibling of the column, so the browser never compares 40 against 20: it paints the whole isolated column, toast included, against the bar as a single unit, and the column loses. Raising the toast to z-50 inside the column would have changed nothing, which is the trap here. Fix: the toast wrapper moved out of the isolated column and is now a sibling of the sticky bar, so both live in the same context and z-50 beats z-20 for real. The reported photos screen renders its region at shell level already, which is why it looked fine. The offset went from top-4 to top-20, an 80px anchor against the 56px bar, giving the 24px of air the review asked for, both values off the 4px scale. ToastRegion itself needed no change: it carries no positioning of its own, only w-80 and gap-2, so the parent owns placement. Verified with npx tsc --noEmit, clean. A unit test would assert class strings here rather than paint order, which is not worth having, so the check is the typecheck plus the visual review at 200% zoom where the bar and the toast no longer overlap. Root cause: trackShortcut is a fire-and-forget call with no .catch on it. It returns the postTelemetry promise and every call site drops that promise on the floor, so a 502 from the analytics endpoint became an unhandled rejection. The app's window unhandledrejection listener treats anything that reaches it as a fatal app error and swaps in the full-screen error card, which is the red card the coordinators described, and because that card mounts over the checklist the browser moves focus to the document body - hence losing their place in the list. The checklist writes were never affected, which matches Dana's note that the ticks are all there after a reload.

Fix is in the helper, not the call site. There are six trackShortcut callers across the checklist, stage nav, document tray and command bar; guarding one of them would have left the other five able to nuke the screen the same way. trackShortcut now voids the promise with a .catch that hands the error to reportBackground, so telemetry failures stay in the background channel where they belong and never surface as an app crash. Return type goes from Promise<void> to void, which is what the call sites already assumed.

Verified with the onboarding suite. The 502 stub that the checklist test uses still fires, but the rejection no longer escapes the test file, so the suite goes from 1 error to green with the same six assertions it always had.

findings.detail:
Root cause: the 3px width was written as a plain arbitrary-value utility and lost to a variant of the same property. The cell class carried both outline-[3px] and focus-visible:outline-1. Tailwind compiles the arbitrary one to a bare class selector, and compiles the variant to that class plus a :focus-visible pseudo-class. The variant selector is the more specific of the two, so the moment the cell actually has keyboard focus the 1px rule wins on outline-width. Where the class sits in the attribute makes no difference, which is why it looked correct in the source. Hover was never affected because nothing there touches outline-width, and the colour and offset survived because no variant competes for those two properties.

Fix: state the width in the same state the design spec talks about. The two competing widths are replaced by a single focus-visible:outline-[3px], with the colour and offset left unconditional. One rule now sets outline-width in the focused state, so there is nothing to out-specify.

Verified in a real browser rather than jsdom, since this is a specificity question and only a computed style can answer it: the playwright spec arrows from 1 June to 2 June and reads getComputedStyle(node).outlineWidth, which is now 3px.

The existing handler called navigator.clipboard.writeText(...).then(...) with no catch and no unmount guard. Two problems fell out of adding feedback to it. findings.detail:
The chip built its classes by interpolation: `bg-${tone}-100`, `text-${tone}-800`, `bg-${tone}-600` and the dark variants, with `tone` coming out of `STATUS_TONES`. Tailwind scans source files for complete class strings, so `bg-emerald-100` never appears anywhere for it to find and none of those rules are emitted into the production stylesheet. The dev server serves a much wider set, which is exactly why it looked right there and flat in the build.

The refactor is a swap of the indirection: instead of a map of colour names glued into class strings at render, there are two maps of complete class strings, `STATUS_CHIP_CLASSES` and `STATUS_DOT_CLASSES`, keyed by the same `CleanroomStatus` union, so a missing status is a type error rather than a silently empty class. `tone` is gone; nothing in the file builds a class name any more.

The chip already carried its own words - `STATUS_TEXT` renders "Ready for entry", "Work in progress" or "Blocked, see bay log" next to the bay label - and that is untouched, so the printed bay log still distinguishes the three without colour.
